summary: This RFC explains how to use Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm keys and signatures in DNSSEC. It lists the curves to be used and specifies SHA-2 hashes for the signatures. Elliptic curves give strong signatures with smaller keys than older schemes.

eli5.summary: DNSSEC puts a tamper-proof seal on DNS answers. This RFC lets the seal be made with a newer kind of math that gives a strong seal using a smaller stamp.

questions: how to use ecdsa in dnssec
subtitle: Defines ECDSA with the P-256 and P-384 curves as DNSSEC signing algorithms, plus SHA-384 DS records.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC's most popular signature algorithm was RSA with SHA-1 using 1024 or 2048-bit keys, and DNSSEC has to store and transmit both keys and signatures, which are large with RSA.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines DNSKEY and RRSIG formats for ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256 (algorithm 13) and with P-384 and SHA-384 (algorithm 14), and defines a SHA-384 digest type (4) for DS records.
tldr.outcome: ECDSA keys and signatures are much shorter than RSA ones, and signing is faster, though validation is slower. Conformant implementations MUST support both algorithms.

today: RFC 6605 is a Proposed Standard from April 2012. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Add ECDSA to DNSSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC, defined in RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, uses cryptographic keys and digital signatures to authenticate DNS data. When this RFC was written, the most popular signature algorithm was RSA with SHA-1, using keys of 1024 or 2048 bits.

This document defines the DNSKEY and RRSIG resource records for two new signing algorithms: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve DSA) with curve P-256 and SHA-256, and ECDSA with curve P-384 and SHA-384. It also defines the DS record for the SHA-384 hash; the DS record for SHA-256 is already defined in RFC 4509.
sections.eli5: DNSSEC needs a secret stamp to prove an answer is genuine. This note adds two newer kinds of stamp to the list of allowed ones.

sections.title: Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC says ECDSA with P-256 has roughly the strength of RSA with 3072-bit keys. ECDSA keys are much shorter (256 versus 3072 bits) and so are its signatures, which matters because DNSSEC stores and transmits both.

In both algorithms the elliptic curve size is matched to the hash output size, based on the widespread belief that each has strength equal to half its length. Matching prevents an attacker from choosing the weaker half. By contrast, RSA with 2048-bit keys and SHA-256 has a signing portion significantly weaker than its hash portion.

There is a speed trade-off. Signing with ECDSA is significantly faster than with RSA (over 20 times in some implementations), but validating RSA signatures is significantly faster than validating ECDSA ones (about 5 times in some implementations).
sections.eli5: The new stamp is tiny and quick to make, but a little slower to check. The RFC also makes sure the stamp and the fingerprint are equally hard to fake.

sections.title: Curves and SHA-384 DS Records
sections.content:
Signer and verifier must agree on the ECDSA parameters. The RFC uses the NIST curves P-256 (FIPS 186-3 Section D.1.2.3) and P-384 (Section D.1.2.4), which are the same as the 256-bit and 384-bit random ECP groups in RFC 5114.

SHA-384 for DS records follows the SHA-256 implementation in RFC 4509, except that the underlying algorithm is SHA-384, the digest value is 48 bytes long, and the digest type code is 4.
sections.eli5: Both sides must use the same math settings, like two people playing a game by the same rulebook. The RFC names the exact rulebook pages.

sections.title: DNSKEY and RRSIG Encoding
sections.content:
An ECDSA public key is a single value called Q in FIPS 186-3. In a DNSSEC key, Q is a simple bit string for the uncompressed form of a curve point, x | y.

An ECDSA signature is two non-negative integers, r and s. Each is formatted as an octet string and they are joined as the concatenation r | s. For P-256, each integer MUST be encoded as 32 octets; for P-384, each MUST be 48 octets.

Conformant implementations that create records for the DNS MUST implement signing and verification for both algorithms, and conformant DNSSEC verifiers MUST implement verification for both.
sections.eli5: The key is a point on a curve written as two numbers glued together. The signature is also two numbers glued together, each always the same fixed length.

sections.title: Algorithm Numbers and NSEC3
sections.content:
Algorithm number 13 means ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256 (mnemonic ECDSAP256SHA256), and number 14 means ECDSA with P-384 and SHA-384 (ECDSAP384SHA384). DS digest type 4 means SHA-384 and has status OPTIONAL.

Unlike RFC 5155, which created separate algorithm identifiers to signal NSEC3 support, this document defines no such aliases. A validator that implements these algorithms MUST be able to validate negative answers using both NSEC and NSEC3 with hash algorithm 1. An authoritative server that does not implement NSEC3 MAY still serve zones using these algorithms with NSEC denial of existence.
sections.eli5: Each kind of stamp has a number so everyone knows which one was used. These new stamps work whichever way the server proves a name does not exist.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content: The RFC includes complete examples for each curve: a private key in v1.2 format, a DNSKEY for example.net. with flags 257 and protocol 3, a DS record, and a signed www.example.net. A record with its RRSIG. The P-256 example uses key tag 55648 and the P-384 example uses key tag 10771.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows real sample keys and signatures so builders can check their own work against them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The work factor of ECDSA with P-256 or P-384 is generally considered equivalent to half the key size, 128 bits and 192 bits respectively. The RFC notes that this could change if better attacks are found. The security considerations in RFC 4509 also apply.

IANA added digest type 4 (SHA-384, OPTIONAL) to the DS digest registry, and algorithm numbers 13 and 14 (both with Zone Signing marked Y) to the DNSSEC algorithm numbers registry. For Transaction Security, the RFC says there has been no determination of standardization.
sections.eli5: The new stamps are thought to be as hard to fake as a 128-bit or 192-bit lock, though that could change if clever attacks are discovered.
